articles.title: Researchers blasted discarded wind turbine blades with electricity at 2,000°C for half a second, turning difficult-to-recycle waste into a graphene-rich material that could strengthen new turbine blades
articles.summary: Wind turbines are often seen as one of the cleaner ways to generate electricity.
articles.body: Wind turbines are often seen as one of the cleaner ways to generate electricity. Their towering structures and enormous blades have become familiar sights across landscapes, harnessing something as simple as the wind to produce power. But what happens when these machines grow old? While generating renewable energy is one part of the sustainability conversation, dealing with the waste left behind is another.Wind turbine blades are built to withstand years of strong winds, rain, extreme temperatures and constant movement. Unfortunately, their durability also makes them incredibly difficult to dispose of once they reach the end of their working lives. Many retired blades are still sent to landfills, creating a waste problem that the renewable energy industry has yet to fully solve.Researchers at Tsinghua University in China may have found a rather unusual way to tackle this problem. They have developed a technique that uses an intense burst of electricity to heat discarded wind turbine blade material to around 2,000°C in just half a second. The process transforms the waste into two valuable materials, silicon carbide and graphene, which could potentially be used to make stronger wind turbine blades.Why are old wind turbine blades so difficult to recycle?Wind turbines generally have a service life of around 20 years. Once they are too old or damaged to operate safely, their blades need to be replaced. However, unlike many everyday plastic products, these enormous structures cannot simply be melted down and reshaped into something new.Most wind turbine blades are made using glass fibres embedded in a material called thermoset resin. The fibres provide structural strength, while the resin holds everything together. During manufacturing, the resin undergoes a chemical process called curing, which creates permanent molecular bonds. This makes the material strong enough to withstand years of mechanical stress, but also prevents it from being melted and reused like conventional plastics.Existing recycling methods have their own limitations. One common approach is pyrolysis, which uses high temperatures to break down the resin and recover other materials. However, the process can damage or weaken the recovered fibres. Mechanical recycling, meanwhile, involves shredding the blades into smaller pieces, which often limits how the resulting material can be reused.This leaves manufacturers with a rather difficult question: how do you recycle something that was specifically designed not to break down easily?A powerful electrical pulse transforms the wasteThe research team, led by Bing Deng, approached the problem by looking at what the blades were already made of. Their glass fibres contain silica, while the resin is rich in carbon. Instead of trying to separate these components and preserve their original forms, the researchers found a way to transform them into something else.First, they collected retired wind turbine blades from a wind farm in southern China and ground the material into a fine powder. This was mixed with carbon black, a form of carbon that helps conduct electricity. The mixture was then placed inside a quartz tube between graphite electrodes.The team used a technique known as flash Joule heating, which passes a powerful electrical current through a material, producing an extremely rapid rise in temperature. In this experiment, the mixture reached approximately 2,000°C (3,632°F) in just 0.5 seconds.At such high temperatures, the silica from the glass fibres reacts with carbon to form silicon carbide, a hard and heat-resistant compound. Meanwhile, the carbon from the resin reorganises into graphene, a material made up of extremely thin layers of carbon atoms. Graphene is particularly valued for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity.The result is a mixture of silicon carbide and functionalised graphene that can be recovered and used as an additive in fresh epoxy resin. Interestingly, the process does not require additional solvents or chemical catalysts to bring about this transformation.Could this make future wind turbine blades stronger?The researchers did not stop at producing these materials. They also wanted to find out whether the recovered mixture could actually improve the performance of new materials.They added small quantities of the silicon carbide-graphene mixture to fresh epoxy resin and tested the resulting samples for strength and stiffness. At an addition of just 0.3% by weight, the resin showed an approximately 11% increase in tensile strength and a 27% increase in tensile stiffness compared with unmodified resin. Its bending strength also increased by around 6%.The researchers found another interesting benefit. Adding just 0.1% of the recovered material increased the resin's thermal diffusivity by approximately 41%. In simple terms, this measures how quickly heat spreads through a material.This could be particularly useful for wind turbine blades, which operate in changing weather conditions. Ice accumulation, for instance, can affect their performance in colder regions. Materials that distribute heat more efficiently could potentially help address some of these challenges.However, it is important to understand that these improvements were demonstrated in laboratory resin samples, not complete turbine blades. More testing will be needed to establish how the material performs in actual turbine structures.A more affordable way to deal with turbine waste?Beyond the material itself, the researchers also examined whether the process could make economic and environmental sense.Their life-cycle assessment estimated that the technique could produce around 83% fewer greenhouse gas emissions than a thermal recycling route with heat recovery, and approximately 92% fewer emissions than chemical dissolution using nitric acid.A preliminary economic analysis also suggested that processing a tonne of discarded blade material could generate a net benefit of around $80. For comparison, the researchers estimated costs of approximately $460 per tonne for pyrolysis and $1,800 per tonne for chemical dissolution.These figures, however, are based on laboratory-scale assessments and modelling. They do not yet establish the actual costs or profits of running an industrial recycling facility.For now, the biggest challenge is scaling up the technology. Most experiments used very small quantities of material, with larger demonstrations reaching 10 grams. The researchers are working towards processing much larger quantities and testing the recovered material in actual turbine blades.Renewable energy is meant to offer a cleaner alternative to conventional power sources, but its sustainability cannot end with electricity generation. What happens to the infrastructure after it has served its purpose matters just as much. If this technique can eventually work on an industrial scale, discarded turbine blades may no longer have to be treated as the end of a product's life. They could become the raw material for the next generation.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: A critically endangered leatherback turtle tried to nest on an Ecuador sidewalk before finding a quieter beach; researchers tracked 146 eggs from her season and saw 134 hatch, a success rate of 91.8%
articles.summary: In January, under the light of a full moon and one too many streetlights, a critically endangered leatherback turtle named Bella did something both
articles.body: In January, under the light of a full moon and one too many streetlights, a critically endangered leatherback turtle named Bella did something both remarkable and worrying: she tried to nest on a sidewalk in Ecuador.Disoriented by nearby streetlights, the enormous female crawled over a rock breakwater and left the beach behind. She failed to lay her eggs there and returned to the ocean, still carrying them. Two nights later, she tried again, this time on a quieter stretch of sand at Playa de Crucita. There, she dug a nest, deposited 47 eggs, covered them carefully, and returned to the sea.A few weeks later, 44 hatchlings emerged and made their way toward the surf. Bella, it turned out, was only beginning. Researchers who had tagged her during her first attempt found that she nested four or five times during the 2026 season. Across all her nests, 146 eggs produced 134 hatchlings, i.e. a 91.8% success rate.For a species whose eastern Pacific population has fallen by more than 90% since the 1980s, that number is a small but powerful sign that leatherbacks may still be able to adapt, if people give them the space and protection to do so.A species on the edgeLeatherback turtles are the largest sea turtles on Earth, capable of reaching up to three metres in length and weighing as much as a tonne. They are extraordinary travellers: unlike most sea turtles, they thrive in both warm and cold waters, migrating thousands of kilometres from tropical nesting beaches to feeding grounds in cooler, subpolar parts of the Pacific, where they feed largely on jellyfish.But the eastern Pacific leatherback population is in serious trouble. Decades of fishing bycatch, plastic pollution, vessel strikes, egg harvesting and loss of nesting habitat have combined with climate-driven pressures to push the species toward collapse. Scientists warn that, without major intervention, the eastern Pacific subspecies could disappear within 60 years.Ecuador becomes unexpected habitatA new study led in part by Simon Fraser University marine eco-toxicologist Juan José Alava found a record-breaking number of eastern Pacific leatherback nests along several Ecuadorian beaches during the 2025–2026 nesting season. These beaches lie more than 1,000 miles south of the species’ usual nesting grounds in Mexico and Costa Rica.Historically, seeing a reproductive female leatherback on Ecuador’s coast was rare. Now, researchers believe the turtles may be adapting their reproductive cycles to take advantage of Ecuador’s coastline, particularly during cooler La Niña periods in the southeastern tropical Pacific.The researchers reviewed more than 45 years of records, including sightings of adult females, nests, hatching success, nesting attempts and strandings. They compared these records with El Niño and La Niña events, which cause major swings in sea-surface temperatures.They found that leatherback activity and nesting in Ecuador increased during cooler La Niña episodes over the past decade. Even more importantly, the number of eggs per nest and hatching rates in Ecuador were comparable to those in the turtles’ traditional nesting grounds. In some cases, Ecuadorian nests produced more hatchlings than usual.That does not mean climate change is good for leatherbacks. Rather, it suggests that some turtles may be responding to warming and shifting ocean conditions by seeking out cooler coastal areas where reproduction can still succeed. It is adaptation, but it is also a warning: species are being forced to move, and their survival depends on whether the places they move to remain safe.Bella’s first failed nesting attempt reveals another side of the problem. Leatherbacks are powerful swimmers, but on land they are vulnerable, slow and easily confused. Artificial lighting can disorient nesting females and hatchlings, drawing them away from the ocean and toward roads, buildings and other hazards.When Bella encountered streetlights near Playa de Crucita, she left the beach and climbed onto a sidewalk. Had conditions been different, she could have been injured, stranded, or unable to lay her eggs at all. Instead, she returned to the sea and found a quieter location two nights later.Conservation thus includes managing the everyday edges of coastal towns: reducing light pollution, keeping beaches clear and accessible, controlling vehicle access, and ensuring that nesting females are not disturbed.From hatchlings to hopeEcuador’s role in leatherback conservation is not entirely new. In 2021, nine leatherbacks hatched after their eggs were artificially incubated at Punta Bikini beach in Manabí province. Earlier that year, 60 leatherbacks had also hatched in the region. Before those successes, nests found along the Ecuadorian coast in 2015 and 2017 had not produced hatchlings.The difference now is scale and consistency. Bella’s 91.8% hatching success, alongside the wider increase in nesting activity, suggests that Ecuador may be becoming more than an occasional stopover. It may be emerging as a meaningful secondary nesting area for a population that desperately needs options.Still, researchers caution against treating this as a victory lap. A good nesting season cannot undo decades of decline. Leatherbacks face dangers long before they reach a beach and long after hatchlings enter the water: fishing nets, plastic debris, boat traffic, changing food supplies and warming oceans all remain serious threats.What needs to happen nextThe study’s authors argue that protecting Ecuador’s beaches must become a priority. That means sustained monitoring, effective coastal-zone management, efforts to reduce fishing bycatch, and conservation plans developed with local communities and Indigenous and traditional knowledge holders.It also means protecting the conditions that made Bella’s second attempt successful: dark, quiet beaches; safe nesting habitat; and hatcheries or relocation programmes only when genuinely necessary. Conservation works best when it supports natural behaviour rather than replacing it.Bella’s 134 hatchlings are not guaranteed to survive. Many will face predators, fishing gear, pollution and an ocean that is changing faster than evolution can comfortably respond. But their emergence is proof that the species is not finished yet.A turtle that briefly mistook a sidewalk for a nesting beach, then found her way back to the sand, has given scientists and conservationists something rare: hope grounded in evidence. The challenge now is to make sure that, next nesting season, Bella and turtles like her find safe beaches waiting for them, not lights, roads and obstacles.Your child uses AI every day.
